title: Kasa Syntax & Language Fundamentals
intro: This teaches the actual Kasa syntax using the maintained language contract. It includes grammar patterns, a worked program, another runnable example, line-by-line reasoning, practice and mistakes. Treat the contract as a candidate until interpreter parity gates finish.

units.title: Writing Kasa source: lines, comments and names
units.why: A computer cannot guess your instructions. Learn exactly what counts as a statement, comment and identifier.
units.rule: Comments begin with #; a line ends a statement; names are case-sensitive; source files use UTF-8.
units.example:
# This line explains our program
ma school = "Akwaaba"
ka school
units.walkthrough: Read ka followed by a string; the interpreter prints it and ends the line. A comment is ignored. The name school is assigned before it is used.
units.practice: Write a greeting for your school, add a comment explaining it, then change the variable name consistently.
units.experiment: Try to use School instead of school in the print statement. Explain why the unknown-name error appears.
units.caution: Comments do not run. Kasa keywords are case-sensitive and spaces used for indentation do not define blocks.
tokens: Starts a comment lasting until the end of the line
trace: The comment is ignored by the interpreter.
ma school evaluates the quoted string and associates it with school.
ka school retrieves and prints the value.
units.fix: Names are case-sensitive: School and school are different. Use the assigned spelling.
units.challenge: Why does ka school work after ma school = "Akwaaba"? What error would happen if the assignment moved below the print?
units.bridge: Every programming language has lexical rules; Python and JavaScript also distinguish names and strings.

units.title: Printing text and values with ka
units.why: A program can tell a learner what it calculated, but only when asked to print.
units.rule: The ka keyword evaluates an expression and displays its value followed by a newline.
units.secondExample:
ka "I am learning Kasa"
ka "Second message"
units.secondOutput:
I am learning Kasa
Second message
units.walkthrough: The quoted value is text. The arithmetic expression 4 + 3 produces the number 7. Each ka starts a new output line.
units.practice: Print three different messages and one arithmetic result. Predict all output lines first.
units.experiment: Try ka "4 + 3". Why does the result look different from ka 4 + 3?
units.caution: Printing is different from assigning a value. Text inside quotes is not automatically calculated.
tokens: Adds numeric values or joins compatible text values
trace: ka "Maakye!" evaluates a text literal.
Its displayed characters are Maakye! and the output ends with a newline.
ka 4 + 3 evaluates 4 + 3 before printing the number 7.
units.fix: Quoted characters stay text. Write ka 4 + 3 for arithmetic.
units.challenge: Predict output for ka 10 and ka "10". Why do the outputs look the same although the values have different types?
units.bridge: Printing a value is distinct from the value's data type, regardless of programming language.

units.title: The types: numbers, strings, Boolean and hwee
units.why: Different kinds of information follow different rules; knowing the type prevents surprising mistakes.
units.rule: Kasa has integers, decimal numbers, text, true/false and a no-value marker. Boolean values are not numbers.
units.example:
ka 12
ka 2.5
ka "12"
ka nokware
ka atoro
ka hwee
units.walkthrough: The display of number 12 and text "12" looks alike, but the values behave differently when you calculate. Boolean nokware and atoro represent logical truth.
units.practice: Classify eight example values into text, number, Boolean and no-value. Explain whether "9" is numeric.
units.experiment: Try a condition using the number 1 where a Boolean is needed. Read the TypeError.
units.caution: A printed representation does not necessarily tell you the original type.
trace: The first statement displays integer 12.
The decimal is displayed as 2.5.
The text "12" has a different type although it displays as 12.
Boolean and no-value literals display their Kasa spellings.
units.fix: Conditions require Boolean, not number. Write sɛ nokware a for a deliberately true branch.
units.challenge: What are the types of 12, "12", nokware, atoro and hwee? Which can be used in arithmetic without conversion?
units.bridge: Kasa's strict Boolean behavior is important when transferring to Python or JavaScript, which have different truthiness rules.

units.title: Variables: ma, names and reassignment
units.why: Store a value, update it, and track how each statement changes the program state.
units.rule: The right side is evaluated first; ma then binds the resulting value to a name. Reassignment updates its current value.
units.example:
ma books = 3
ka books
ma books = books + 2
ka books
units.secondExample:
ma total = 10
ma total = total + 7
ka total
units.walkthrough: At first books means 3. The expression books + 2 produces 5, then ma changes books. The two ka statements display different values.
units.practice: Write code to track donations increasing from 4 books to 9 books.
units.experiment: Try printing a name that has not been assigned. Describe the error and correct it.
units.caution: ma total = total + 7 is an update instruction, not an algebra equation.
tokens: Assigns the right-hand result to the name
trace: books is assigned the integer value 3.
The first ka reads books and prints 3.
books + 2 evaluates to 5 using the existing value.
ma stores 5 back into books, so the second print displays 5.
units.fix: A variable name is required before the assignment operator: ma total = 10.
units.challenge: Trace x after ma x = 2, ma x = x * 3, ma x = x - 1. Explain why the final result is 5.
units.bridge: Assignments are state changes, not equations from mathematics class.

units.title: Arithmetic and operator precedence
units.why: Code uses mathematical rules, not guesses. Changing parentheses can change an answer.
units.rule: Multiplication, division and integer remainder happen before addition/subtraction. Parentheses change evaluation order.
units.walkthrough: 3 * 4 is evaluated before adding 2, giving 14. Parentheses make 2 + 3 run first, giving 20. The remainder of 17 divided by 5 is 2.
units.practice: Write a program that calculates the cost of five exercise books at GHS 7 each plus a one-time GHS 4 delivery charge.
units.experiment: Try dividing by zero and explain why the interpreter rejects it.
units.caution: % uses integers; don't assume decimal floating-point arithmetic is suitable for real accounting or money.
trace: The first line evaluates 3 * 4 before adding 2, yielding 14.
The second line evaluates 2 + 3 inside the parentheses first.
Then 5 * 4 yields 20.
17 % 5 produces the remainder 2.
units.fix: Division by zero is invalid; check the denominator before dividing.
units.challenge: Predict 8 + 2 * 3, (8 + 2) * 3 and 19 % 4, then check with Kasa.
units.bridge: Precedence is shared by most mainstream languages, but numeric overflow and decimal rounding may differ.

units.title: Comparisons: ask precise questions
units.why: A computer makes a decision using a true/false comparison with an exact boundary.
units.rule: Equality uses ==, not assignment =. Comparison produces nokware or atoro. Direct chained comparisons are not supported.
units.example:
ma score = 50
ka score >= 50
ka score > 50
ka score == 50
units.walkthrough: The first rule accepts 50, the second excludes it, and the equality test matches exactly 50. This is why choosing the operator matters.
units.practice: Make a stock alert decision for quantities 9, 10 and 11, with a threshold of ten.
units.experiment: Try 1 < 2 < 3; replace it with separate Boolean comparisons joined by ne.
units.caution: Use separate comparisons and ne rather than assuming Python-style comparison chaining works.
trace: score starts as 50.
score >= 50 evaluates to nokware, so the first print is true.
score > 50 evaluates to atoro because equality is excluded.
score == 50 evaluates to nokware.
units.fix: Chaining comparisons directly is unsupported; use (1 < 2) ne (2 < 3).
units.challenge: For scores 49, 50 and 51, predict >= 50, > 50 and == 50. Build a truth table.
units.bridge: The comparison operators look familiar across languages, but chained comparisons are not portable.

units.title: Boolean logic: ne, anaa and ɛnyɛ
units.why: Sometimes more than one condition matters: permission may require two rules or allow alternatives.
units.syntax: COND ne COND | COND anaa COND | ɛnyɛ COND
units.rule: ne is AND; anaa is OR; ɛnyɛ negates a Boolean. Kasa uses short-circuit evaluation.
units.example:
ka nokware ne atoro
ka nokware anaa atoro
ka ɛnyɛ nokware
units.secondExample:
ma has_book = nokware
ma has_pen = nokware
ka has_book ne has_pen
units.walkthrough: AND is true only when both conditions hold. OR is true when at least one holds. NOT reverses the truth value.
units.practice: Create a classroom supply check using two Boolean variables for book and pen.
units.experiment: Try combining a Boolean with the number 1. Why is the type error useful?
units.caution: Kasa requires real Boolean values. Unlike some host languages, arbitrary numbers or strings are not truth values.
trace: nokware ne atoro is atoro because both are not true.
nokware anaa atoro is nokware because one is true.
ɛnyɛ nokware reverses true to false.
The Boolean operators can avoid evaluating a needless second operand.
units.fix: Use strict Boolean operands such as nokware ne nokware, not numeric truthiness.
units.challenge: Draw all four combinations for A and B. Calculate A ne B and A anaa B for each.
units.bridge: Logical expressions are essential in every language, but type and short-circuit rules need to be learned explicitly.

units.title: Conditions: sɛ ... a, otherwise, awiei
units.why: A conditional selects one of two paths based on a Boolean result.
units.rule: The contextual a after the condition is required. The else branch is optional. Explicit awiei closes the block.
units.example:
ma score = 55
sɛ score >= 50 a
    ka "Pass"
anyɛ_saa_a
    ka "Review"
awiei
units.secondExample:
ma qty = 3
sɛ qty <= 5 a
    ka "Restock"
awiei
units.walkthrough: First the comparison score >= 50 evaluates to nokware. Only the Pass branch executes. The closing awiei is essential even though indentation is for readability.
units.practice: Change score to 49 and to 50 and predict the branch chosen each time.
units.experiment: Remove the a after the condition or awiei. Read the syntax diagnostic, then restore it.
units.caution: Don't teach indentation as the block delimiter: it is visual; Kasa ends nested blocks explicitly with awiei.
tokens: Required conditional marker after the Boolean expression
trace: ma assigns 55 to score.
score >= 50 evaluates to nokware.
The first branch runs and prints Pass.
The else branch is skipped, and awiei ends the conditional.
units.fix: The required a is missing: sɛ score >= 50 a.
units.challenge: Change score to 49, then 50, then 51. Explain exactly which branch runs and why.
units.bridge: The conditional corresponds to if/else in Python and JavaScript, but Kasa has explicit a and awiei markers.

units.title: Counted repetition with mpɛn
units.why: Don't copy identical instructions many times. Use repetition and keep a trace of the running total.
units.rule: The count must be a non-negative integer. The body executes that many times.
units.example:
ma total = 0
mpɛn 4
    ma total = total + 5
awiei
ka total
units.secondExample:
mpɛn 3
    ka "Sɛ wo ho te sɛn?"
awiei
units.secondOutput:
Sɛ wo ho te sɛn?
Sɛ wo ho te sɛn?
Sɛ wo ho te sɛn?
units.walkthrough: The total starts at zero. Four executions add 5, so it changes 0 → 5 → 10 → 15 → 20. It prints once after the loop ends.
units.practice: Change the repetition count to six and the contribution to three. Check the result on paper.
units.experiment: Try mpɛn -2 and explain why a negative repetition count is invalid.
units.caution: The loop repeats the body, not necessarily the output. You only print when ka is executed.
trace: total begins at 0.
The four passes produce totals 5, 10, 15 and 20.
After the fourth pass, execution exits the loop.
ka total prints 20 only once.
units.fix: The repeat count must be a nonnegative integer.
units.challenge: Trace total for five repetitions of +4, writing down the value after each pass.
units.bridge: Counted loops train the same fundamental repetition reasoning found in for loops elsewhere.

units.title: Conditional repetition with bere_a
units.why: Use a while loop when you cannot know in advance how many times a task will repeat.
units.rule: The condition must be Boolean; it is checked before each iteration. Ensure the program changes something that allows it to become false.
units.example:
ma count = 1
bere_a count <= 3
    ka count
    ma count = count + 1
awiei
units.secondExample:
ma n = 0
bere_a n < 2
    ka n
    ma n = n + 1
awiei
units.walkthrough: The loop tests count <= 3 before each pass. The update increases count. When count becomes 4 the condition is false and execution stops.
units.practice: Write a loop printing 2, 4, 6 and 8 using a counter updated inside the body.
units.experiment: Remove the counter update in a safe, small example; explain why the worker time limit exists.
units.caution: A while loop can run zero times. Don't use an always-true condition without a way to stop.
tokens: A Boolean reevaluated before each iteration
trace: count begins at 1.
Before pass 1, 1 <= 3 is true; it prints 1, then increments.
Passes 2 and 3 print 2 and 3 while updating the counter.
At count 4, the test fails and the loop stops.
units.invalid:
ma n = 1
bere_a n <= 3
    ka n
awiei
units.fix: The counter never changes, so the loop does not naturally stop. Update n in the body.
units.challenge: Modify the counter so the loop prints 2, 4, 6 and 8 without printing 10.
units.bridge: While loops are useful across languages; termination requires reasoning about changing state.

units.title: Break and continue: gyae and toa_so
units.why: Sometimes a loop should stop early or skip one pass when a condition is met.
units.rule: gyae ends the nearest loop. toa_so skips to the next iteration. Use these only within a loop.
units.example:
ma n = 0
bere_a n < 5
    ma n = n + 1
    sɛ n == 3 a
        gyae
    awiei
    ka n
awiei
units.secondExample:
ma n = 0
bere_a n < 3
    ma n = n + 1
    sɛ n == 2 a
        toa_so
    awiei
    ka n
awiei
units.walkthrough: The loop advances n before checking the break. At n = 3, gyae exits before printing 3. The second example skips the print when n is 2.
units.practice: Create a loop that stops after printing numbers through 4.
units.experiment: Move toa_so above the counter update; discuss how that can create an endless loop.
units.caution: Always update state before continuing when necessary for loop termination.
tokens: Used to decide when to break or continue
trace: n increases at the start of each loop pass.
At n=1, the condition is false, so 1 prints.
At n=2, the condition is false, so 2 prints.
At n=3, gyae stops the loop before the print statement.
units.fix: gyae only makes sense inside an active loop; put it in a loop conditional.
units.challenge: Show how the output changes when gyae is replaced with toa_so. Why must the increment happen first?
units.bridge: Break and continue exist in many languages, but Kasa's keyword spellings are its own.

units.title: Functions: dwumadie, parameters, sanma
units.why: Write a calculation once, call it with several values and reuse the returned result.
units.rule: A function definition stores code. Calling passes arguments; sanma returns a value. Without an explicit return the result is hwee.
units.example:
dwumadie total(qty, price)
    sanma qty * price
awiei
ka total(3, 7)
ka total(2, 5)
units.secondExample:
dwumadie add(a, b)
    sanma a + b
awiei
ka add(4, 6)
units.walkthrough: The first call binds qty=3 and price=7 in a local environment, returning 21. The second call reuses the function definition with different arguments.
units.practice: Make a function to calculate a simple transport fare for passengers and ticket price.
units.experiment: Call a function with too many or too few arguments. Explain the arity error.
units.caution: Returning is different from printing. A function's local variables are not automatically global.
tokens: Names the function and its parameter list
Returns a value to the caller
trace: Defining total stores reusable instructions; it does not print.
The call total(3, 7) binds the two parameter values.
sanma returns 3 * 7 = 21 to the caller, which prints it.
The call total(2, 5) reuses the same function, returning 10.
units.invalid:
dwumadie total(qty, price)
    ka qty * price
awiei
ka total(3, 7)
units.fix: ka inside the function prints, but without sanma the function returns hwee. Use sanma for a reusable result.
units.challenge: Write a function that adds a fixed fee to a base price, then call it with two different amounts.
units.bridge: Function definitions and parameters translate conceptually to Python def and JavaScript function syntax.

units.title: Lists: brackets, zero-based indexing and length
units.why: Organize several related values without inventing a new variable name for each one.
units.rule: Items begin at index 0; a three-item list has indices 0, 1, 2. tentɛn returns the number of elements.
units.example:
ma prices = [5, 10, 15]
ka prices[0]
ka prices[2]
ka tentɛn(prices)
units.walkthrough: Index 0 selects 5; index 2 selects 15. The number of entries is three, so tentɛn(prices) returns 3.
units.practice: Make a list of four prices and print the second and fourth values.
units.experiment: Try prices[3] for a three-item list. Explain the index error.
units.caution: Indices must be integers and in range; negative indexing is not supported as a shortcut for the final item.
tokens: Reads an element at a zero-based position
trace: prices holds three entries in a fixed order.
prices[0] retrieves the first entry, 5.
prices[2] retrieves the third entry, 15.
tentɛn(prices) returns 3, the number of entries.
units.fix: With three entries, only 0, 1 and 2 are valid indices. Position 3 does not exist.
units.challenge: Create a list of four scores; print its second value, last value and length.
units.bridge: Zero-based list indexing is used by Python, JavaScript arrays and many other languages.

units.title: Changing list elements
units.why: Lists can be updated, letting a program represent a changing collection of values.
units.rule: A valid zero-based index can be assigned a new value using ma, changing that list element.
units.example:
ma prices = [5, 10, 15]
ma prices[1] = 12
ka prices[1]
ka prices
units.secondExample:
ma books = [2, 4, 6]
ma books[0] = 3
ka books[0]
units.walkthrough: The first index begins at zero, so prices[1] is the second entry. The update changes 10 to 12 but preserves the other entries.
units.practice: Start with three product quantities, replace the final quantity, and display the full list.
units.experiment: Try to assign prices[8]; identify why there is no element at that position.
units.caution: Changing a list item is not the same as creating a new list; this changes the existing collection.
trace: prices begins as [5, 10, 15].
ma prices[1] = 12 changes only the second entry.
ka prices[1] prints 12.
ka prices displays the entire modified list.
units.fix: The target index must exist in the list; changing an item cannot create skipped positions.
units.challenge: Record three fictional school supply counts, update the first and last, then print the list.
units.bridge: Understanding mutation prepares learners to reason about state changes and side effects in larger programs.

units.title: Built-ins: bisa, tentɛn, nɔma and nsɛm
units.why: Programs must sometimes read a line, count characters, convert numeric input or build a printed label.
units.rule: Built-ins are callable names. bisа reads text input; nɔma converts numeric text; nsɛm converts a value to display text.
units.example:
ma qty = nɔma("5")
ma price = 7
ka "Total GHS: " + nsɛm(qty * price)
ka tentɛn([1, 2, 3])
units.walkthrough: The text "5" becomes the numeric 5, which can be multiplied by 7. nsɛm makes the total printable beside text. tentɛn counts three entries.
units.practice: Use bisa() to ask for a fictional product quantity, convert it with nɔma and compute a total.
units.experiment: Try nɔma("twelve") and observe the conversion error. What would a real form need to do?
units.caution: Kasa does not currently provide imports, file I/O, networking, classes or currency-safe decimal arithmetic in its core grammar.
tokens: Reads the next supplied input line
Converts supported numeric text to a number
Converts a value to display text
trace: nɔma("5") produces numeric 5.
qty * price calculates 5 * 7 = 35.
nsɛm converts 35 to the text needed for the label.
tentɛn([1,2,3]) produces 3.
units.fix: The input text is not a valid numeric representation. Use a numeric string such as "5".
units.challenge: Ask for a fictional number of notebooks with bisa(), convert it, and calculate the cost at GHS 3 each.
units.bridge: These are Kasa built-ins; other languages have different function names and input rules.

units.title: Syntax errors and diagnostic thinking
units.why: A good programmer learns to read an error rather than restarting everything.
units.syntax: Read line and location; identify SyntaxError, TypeError, IndexError or runtime errors.
units.rule: Errors are evidence. Syntax rules are different from type rules; correct one cause at a time.
units.walkthrough: If the source lacks an awiei, it is malformed. If you divide by zero, the parser may accept the source but execution fails. If you use a name you never declared, the interpreter reports an unknown name.
units.practice: Deliberately make and fix three different errors, recording the initial problem and solution.
units.experiment: Try ka 1 / 0 then fix the denominator. Explain the difference between a syntax and runtime error.
units.caution: The web interpreter intentionally has resource and time limits. A green sample-output check tests only that example.
tokens: Operation used with the wrong kind of value
trace: ma total = 3 assigns a numeric value.
ka total + 2 evaluates to 5.
The interpreter prints 5 and a newline.
If the source were incomplete or a type mismatched, errors would explain what failed.
units.fix: Declare a name with ma first, or correct the spelling. Read the reported location and category.
units.challenge: Write and fix an unknown-name error, a type error and a missing awiei error. Keep notes describing each fix.
units.bridge: Debugging is a transferable habit: observe, hypothesize, change one thing, and verify.
